lessons.title: Where Every Data Point Lives: Annual Reports, BSE/NSE Filings and screener.in

body.text: Every governance signal in this course is free, public, and filed in a predictable place. The only scarce resource is knowing which document answers which question.

children.text: Indian disclosure rules are demanding by global standards. Listed companies file results, shareholding patterns, corporate governance reports, related party transactions, encumbrance details, material events, and voting outcomes, all on a fixed calendar, all available to you at no cost. The reason most investors never use any of it is not secrecy. It is that nobody tells you where to look. This lesson is that map.
The Four Sources, and What Each Is Good For

cells: screener.in
Ten years of financials, ratios, shareholding and pledge trends, and links to annual reports, concalls, and credit ratings in one place
Summarised data only; it does not carry notes to accounts, board details, or voting results

Published once a year, so it is always somewhat dated
BSE and NSE filings
Everything that happens between annual reports: results, shareholding, encumbrance, material events, voting results, auditor changes
Search interfaces are built for compliance, not for reading
Regulator and rating agency sites

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Start every company here. The Documents section links to annual reports, concall transcripts, credit rating reports, and investor presentations, so you rarely need to hunt on the company website.

body.label: BSE Corporate Filings
body.description: Search by company name for corporate announcements, shareholding patterns with promoter-wise pledge details, voting results, and encumbrance disclosures.

children.text: Reading an Annual Report in the Right Order

An Indian annual report is designed to be read front to back: glossy pages, chairman's message, business highlights, then the financials at the end. For governance work, read it backwards. The parts written under legal obligation come first, and the parts written by the marketing department come last, if at all.

body.caption: The governance reading order for an annual report

cells: Independent Auditor's Report and CARO annexure
Can the numbers be relied on at all?
Related party disclosures note
How much business runs through promoter entities, and what is outstanding?
Contingent liabilities and commitments note
What guarantees and claims sit off the balance sheet?
Corporate Governance Report
Board composition, independence, attendance, pay, and any penalties in the last three years
Board's Report annexures: AOC-1, AOC-2, secretarial audit, pay particulars
Subsidiary financials, related party contracts, compliance qualifications, pay ratios
Cash flow statement and accounting policies
Does profit turn into cash, and how aggressive are the choices?
Management Discussion and Analysis, chairman's letter
What management says about the year, to compare with everything above

body.text: Two annexures to the Board's Report are underused. Form AOC-1 gives each subsidiary's capital, net worth, turnover, and profit, so you can see which group companies are losing money. Form AOC-2 lists related party contracts, often with more description of the arrangement than the accounting note provides. Together they answer most questions about where cash goes inside a group.

points: Related party transactions, balances, and loans
Auditor opinion wording, Key Audit Matters, and CARO remarks
Board composition, tenure, attendance, and pay
Voting results and proxy advisory concerns
Encumbrance details, material events, and regulatory actions

children.text: One underused free source belongs alongside these: credit rating rationales from agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, and India Ratings. They are published for every rated borrower and often describe group exposures, support to weak group companies, and refinancing risk in plainer language than any company document. If a promoter group is under pressure, a rating rationale usually says so before the share price does.

body.label: SEBI Orders and Enforcement
body.description: Search by company or individual name for adjudication orders, whole-time member orders, interim directions, and settlement orders, then check any appeal outcome at the Securities Appellate Tribunal.

body.caption: A repeatable hour, mapped to the 20 checks

cells: 0 to 10
screener.in: ten years of ROCE, profit versus operating cash flow, working capital days, promoter holding and pledge trend
Annual report: auditor's report, CARO annexure, related party note, contingent liabilities
Corporate Governance Report and Board's Report annexures: board, pay, AOC-1, AOC-2, secretarial audit
BSE or NSE: last four quarters of announcements, encumbrance filings, auditor or director changes, voting results
SEBI orders search, plus the latest credit rating rationale for the company and group
Last two investor presentations against the same slides a year earlier, and the statement of deviation if money was raised

body.text: Do this in the order above, not in the order of your curiosity. If the auditor's report or the related party note produces a red line in the first 25 minutes, stop. Continuing to research a company you have already disqualified is how a checklist quietly turns into a justification.

body.title: Which Document Answers the Question?
body.question: You want to know whether a listed company has given corporate guarantees for the borrowings of a promoter-owned company that is not its subsidiary. Where do you look first?
options: The contingent liabilities note and the related party note in the annual report
The chairman's letter in the annual report
body.explanation: Guarantees are not debt, so they never appear in the borrowings line or in screener.in's ratios. They sit in the contingent liabilities note, and the related party note tells you which of them were given for promoter entities. Quarterly results and the chairman's letter will not mention them.

body.title: Name the Annexure
body.textWithBlank: Form ___ is the annexure to the Board's Report that gives the capital, net worth, turnover, and profit of every subsidiary, associate, and joint venture.
body.explanation: Form AOC-1 is the fastest way to see which group companies are loss-making and how much of the group's assets sit outside the listed parent. Its companion, Form AOC-2, lists related party contracts and arrangements.

body.title: Twenty Minutes Before the Close
body.scenario: At 2:40 pm you see an exchange filing from a mid cap you hold: the company has announced a preferential issue of shares and warrants to promoter group entities, and has also disclosed the resignation of one independent director. The stock is down 7%. You have about 20 minutes before the market closes and cannot complete a full 60-minute pass.
body.prompt: What do you read, in what order, and what decides your action?
body.modelAnswer: Work from the documents that can produce a red line to the ones that only add context. First, open the independent director's resignation letter on the exchange, because the stated reason takes seconds to read and a reference to lack of information, unresolved concerns, or disagreement is decisive on its own. Second, read the preferential issue notice for the allottees, the issue price against today's market price, the share and warrant split, and the stated use of proceeds. Third, on screener.in, check the pledged percentage and cash on the balance sheet, because a company sitting on cash does not need a promoter issue, and a rising pledge explains why the promoter might want one. Fourth, calculate the post-issue promoter stake to see whether control crosses 50%. That is enough to act: if the resignation letter cites concerns, or the issue is at a floor price to promoters with no clear funding need, reduce or exit today rather than waiting. If the letter is routine and the issue funds a disclosed project at a fair price, do nothing today and complete the full pass tonight, including the related party note and the last four quarters of filings.

body.title: Set Up Your Governance Monitoring
steps: Create a watchlist of your holdings on screener.in and check the shareholding and pledge trend each quarter
Bookmark the BSE or NSE announcements page for each holding and scan it weekly for material events
Diarise four dates a year per company: results, shareholding pattern, half-yearly RPT disclosure, and the AGM voting results
Save each year's annual report PDF so you can compare notes and policies year on year
Search SEBI orders for each holding and its promoters once a year
Read the latest credit rating rationale for any company whose promoter group carries debt
Keep your 20-point scorecard sheets in one folder so trends across years are visible at a glance

points: Four sources cover everything: screener.in for trends, the annual report for detail, exchange filings for events, and regulator and rating agency sites for outside verdicts
Read annual reports backwards: auditor's report and CARO, then related party and contingent liability notes, then governance and pay, and the chairman's letter last
Form AOC-1 exposes loss-making subsidiaries and Form AOC-2 describes related party contracts, both in the Board's Report annexures
Between annual reports, the filing calendar gives you shareholding and pledges quarterly, RPTs half-yearly, and material events as they happen
screener.in cannot answer questions about related parties, auditors, boards, or votes, so treat it as the starting point and not the source
A disciplined 60-minute first pass covers all 20 checks, and stopping early when a red line appears is part of the process
